title: Neural Networks
subject: Neural Networks
summary: The mathematics of neural networks, built from the single neuron up: perceptrons and their limits, multilayer networks and universal approximation, loss functions from maximum likelihood, backpropagation derived by hand from the chain rule, reverse-mode automatic differentiation, optimizers, initialization and regularization, and energy-based models. Physical chemistry is the running analogy: softmax is the Boltzmann distribution, gradient descent is overdamped motion on a potential energy surface, saddle points are transition states, and Hopfield networks and Boltzmann machines are the Ising model with its partition function (P7). Coding lives in the optional micrograd project.

units.title: Artificial Neurons and the Perceptron
units.summary: The single neuron as a weighted vote with a threshold, the perceptron learning rule and its limits (XOR), and the smooth sigmoid neuron, whose logistic curve is the same two-state Boltzmann population (Fermi function) the chemist knows from statistical thermodynamics.

lessons.title: The Perceptron as a Linear Threshold Unit
objectives: Compute a perceptron's output from inputs, weights and bias, and rewrite the threshold rule as the sign of w·x + b.
Explain geometrically that the decision boundary w·x + b = 0 is a hyperplane with normal w and offset -b/|w|, and sketch it in 2-D.
Build AND, OR and NAND gates from single perceptrons by choosing weights, and explain why NAND universality makes networks of perceptrons able to compute any Boolean function.

readings.title: Using neural nets to recognize handwritten digits

demoIdeas: Drag the weight vector and bias of a 2-D perceptron and watch the separating line rotate and shift while points recolor by predicted class.

lessons.title: The Perceptron Learning Rule and Its Convergence
objectives: Apply the perceptron update w <- w + eta (y - y_hat) x by hand to a small 2-D data set until it classifies every point correctly.
State the perceptron convergence theorem (at most (R/gamma)^2 mistakes for data separable with margin gamma) and explain what R and gamma measure.
Explain why the rule never settles on non-separable data and why it has no notion of a 'best' separating line.
keyEquations: w \leftarrow w + \eta\,(y - \hat y)\,x,\quad b \leftarrow b + \eta\,(y-\hat y)

readings.title: Using neural nets to recognize handwritten digits

demoIdeas: Step through perceptron updates on a 2-D point cloud: each misclassified point flashes and the boundary jumps; a margin slider shows how fewer steps are needed as the classes separate.

lessons.title: Linear Separability and the XOR Problem
objectives: Prove that no single perceptron computes XOR by showing the four inequalities on w and b are contradictory.
Explain how a fixed nonlinear feature map (e.g. adding x1·x2) makes XOR linearly separable, and why learning such features is the job of hidden layers.

readings.title: Using neural nets to recognize handwritten digits

demoIdeas: Try to place a single line separating the XOR corners (it can't), then toggle a third feature x1·x2 and rotate the 3-D view to see a separating plane appear.

lessons.title: The Sigmoid Neuron: Making Learning Smooth
objectives: Explain why a step activation makes small weight changes produce all-or-nothing output changes, and how the sigmoid fixes this via Δoutput ≈ Σ (∂output/∂w_j) Δw_j + (∂output/∂b) Δb.
Derive σ'(z) = σ(z)(1 - σ(z)) and evaluate where the slope is largest and where the neuron saturates.
Identify the logistic function as the population of the upper state of a two-level system, 1/(1 + e^{ΔE/kT}) (the Fermi function), with z playing the role of -ΔE/kT.

readings.title: Using neural nets to recognize handwritten digits

demoIdeas: Morph a step function into a sigmoid by scaling the weights down, and watch a tiny weight nudge change the output smoothly instead of flipping it.

lessons.title: Activation Functions: Sigmoid, tanh, ReLU and Friends
objectives: Compute and sketch tanh, ReLU, leaky ReLU and softplus with their derivatives, and relate tanh to the sigmoid (tanh z = 2σ(2z) - 1).
Explain why a network with only linear activations collapses to a single linear map, whatever its depth.
Compare activations by saturation (vanishing slope) and by dead units (ReLU with z < 0 always), anticipating the gradient problems of Unit 7.
demoIdeas: Pick an activation from a menu and see the function and its derivative side by side, with the region where the derivative is below 0.05 shaded as 'saturated'.

units.title: Multilayer Networks and What They Can Represent
units.summary: Stacking neurons into layers, written compactly in matrix form; hand-built solutions to XOR; ReLU networks as piecewise-linear functions; the universal approximation theorem and why depth buys exponentially many linear regions.

lessons.title: Feedforward Networks in Matrix Form
objectives: Write the forward pass of a fully connected network layer by layer as a^l = σ(W^l a^{l-1} + b^l), stating the shape of every W^l, b^l and a^l.
Count the parameters of a given architecture (e.g. 784-30-10) and explain what one row of W^l and one column of W^l each represent.

readings.title: Using neural nets to recognize handwritten digits

lectures.title: Chapter 1: But what is a neural network?

demoIdeas: Edit a small network diagram (layer sizes by slider) and see the weight matrices drawn as heat maps with their shapes and the total parameter count update live.

lessons.title: Solving XOR with a Hidden Layer
objectives: Construct, by choosing weights by hand, a 2-2-1 network (ReLU or step units) that computes XOR, and trace all four inputs through it.
Explain the hidden layer as a learned change of coordinates in which the classes become linearly separable.
keyEquations: h = \max(0, Wx + c),\quad y = w^\top h + b

readings.title: Using neural nets to recognize handwritten digits

demoIdeas: Show the four XOR points in input space and, beside it, in hidden-unit space as the learner drags hidden weights; the classes become separable by a line in the right panel.

lessons.title: Shallow ReLU Networks as Piecewise-Linear Functions
objectives: Show that a one-input shallow ReLU network with D hidden units is a piecewise-linear function with at most D joints, and locate each joint at x = -b_d/w_d.
Decompose the network's output into the sum of its hidden units' contributions and adjust weights to fit a given piecewise-linear target.
demoIdeas: Add ReLU hidden units one at a time with sliders for slope and joint position; the summed output curve updates and a target curve shows how close it gets.

lessons.title: Universal Approximation: Bumps, Towers and Their Limits
objectives: Reproduce Nielsen's visual argument: two steep sigmoid units make a 'bump', and a sum of bumps approximates any continuous 1-D function to any accuracy.

State the universal approximation theorem precisely (one hidden layer, continuous target on a compact set, arbitrary ε) and list what it does not promise (how many units, whether gradient descent finds them, generalization).
Extend the construction to two inputs using 'towers' and explain why the number of units can grow exponentially with input dimension.

readings.title: A visual proof that neural nets can compute any function

demoIdeas: Approximate a target curve (e.g. a Morse potential) with N bumps: an N slider and per-bump height sliders show the error shrinking as N grows.

lessons.title: Why Depth? Composition and Linear Regions
objectives: Explain how composing two ReLU networks folds input space, so the number of linear regions can grow exponentially with depth but only polynomially with width.
Compare a shallow and a deep network with the same parameter count by counting their maximum linear regions for a small example.
Argue why depth is an inductive bias toward hierarchical features, not a requirement of representability.

readings.title: Why are deep neural networks hard to train?

demoIdeas: Fold a 1-D input repeatedly: each added layer doubles the number of linear pieces of a sawtooth output, shown alongside a shallow network with the same parameter budget.

units.title: Loss Functions and Gradient Descent
units.summary: Where losses come from (maximum likelihood), softmax and cross-entropy (softmax is the Boltzmann distribution and log-sum-exp is a free energy), and gradient descent as overdamped motion on a potential energy surface, including step-size stability and the noise of minibatches.

lessons.title: Loss Functions from Maximum Likelihood
objectives: Derive mean squared error as the negative log-likelihood of a Gaussian noise model and binary cross-entropy as that of a Bernoulli model.
Apply the recipe 'choose an output distribution, have the network predict its parameters, minimize the negative log-likelihood' to a new case.
demoIdeas: Fit a single parameter to noisy data and toggle between Gaussian and Laplace noise models: the likelihood curve and the implied loss (squared vs absolute error) change together.

lessons.title: Softmax, Cross-Entropy and the Boltzmann Distribution
objectives: Identify the softmax as a Boltzmann distribution over classes with logits z_k = -E_k/kT, and log-sum-exp as -ln Z, i.e. a free energy (up to a factor of kT).
Derive the gradient of softmax cross-entropy with respect to the logits, ∂L/∂z_k = a_k - y_k.
Explain how a temperature parameter sharpens or flattens the softmax, and why subtracting max z before exponentiating changes nothing mathematically but prevents overflow.

readings.title: Improving the way neural networks learn

demoIdeas: Set three logits ('energy levels') and a temperature slider; bar heights show the softmax populations, morphing from uniform at high T to one-hot at low T.

lessons.title: Gradient Descent as Overdamped Motion on a Potential Energy Surface
objectives: Derive the gradient descent update as the forward-Euler discretization of overdamped dynamics γ dθ/dt = -∇L(θ), identifying η = Δt/γ.
Explain why the negative gradient is the direction of steepest descent using the first-order Taylor expansion ΔL ≈ ∇L·Δθ under a fixed step length.
Relate the picture to a geometry optimization on a molecular potential energy surface: minima are stable conformers, and the descent path depends on the starting geometry.

readings.title: Using neural nets to recognize handwritten digits

lectures.title: Chapter 2: Gradient descent, how neural networks learn

demoIdeas: Click anywhere on a 2-D contour map of a double-well 'potential energy surface' to release a ball that rolls downhill under overdamped dynamics; different starting points end in different minima.

lessons.title: Step Size, Curvature and Stability
objectives: Analyze gradient descent on a quadratic bowl L = ½ θᵀHθ in the Hessian's eigenbasis and show each mode shrinks by a factor (1 - ηλ_i) per step.
Derive the stability condition η < 2/λ_max and explain the zigzag and slow progress caused by a large condition number λ_max/λ_min.
Connect this to stiff vibrational modes in a molecule: the stiffest mode limits the stable time step, just as in molecular dynamics.
demoIdeas: On an elongated quadratic bowl, slide the learning rate and watch the path go from crawling, to zigzagging, to diverging at η = 2/λ_max; the bowl's eccentricity is a second slider.

lessons.title: Stochastic and Minibatch Gradient Descent
objectives: Show that the minibatch gradient is an unbiased estimator of the full gradient and that its variance scales as 1/B for batch size B.
Explain epochs, shuffling and why SGD is cheaper per unit progress on large redundant data sets.
Interpret SGD noise as an effective temperature (Langevin dynamics, temperature roughly proportional to η/B) that lets the iterate escape shallow minima.

readings.title: Using neural nets to recognize handwritten digits

demoIdeas: Run full-batch and minibatch descent side by side on the same double-well surface, with a batch-size slider: small batches jitter and sometimes hop the barrier into the deeper well.

units.title: Backpropagation Derived by Hand
units.summary: The four backpropagation equations derived from nothing but the multivariable chain rule, first along a single path, then for full layers; the algorithm, its cost, a full numeric example worked on paper, and why cross-entropy cures the sigmoid's learning slowdown.

lessons.title: The Chain Rule Along a Chain of Single Neurons
objectives: Compute ∂C/∂w for each weight of a 1-1-1-1 chain of sigmoid neurons by multiplying local derivatives along the path.
Explain what each factor (σ'(z), the incoming activation, the downstream weight) contributes and why a deep chain of small σ' factors already hints at vanishing gradients.
keyEquations: \frac{\partial C}{\partial w^{(L)}} = \frac{\partial z^{(L)}}{\partial w^{(L)}}\,\frac{\partial a^{(L)}}{\partial z^{(L)}}\,\frac{\partial C}{\partial a^{(L)}} = a^{(L-1)}\,\sigma'(z^{(L)})\,2(a^{(L)}-y)

lectures.title: Chapter 4: What is backpropagation really doing?

demoIdeas: A chain of four neurons with live values: hover over any weight to light up the path from it to the cost, with each local derivative printed on its edge and their product shown.

lessons.title: The Error δ and the Output-Layer Equation (BP1)
objectives: Define the error of neuron j in layer l as δ_j^l = ∂C/∂z_j^l and explain why z (not a) is the convenient variable.
Derive BP1, δ^L = ∇_a C ⊙ σ'(z^L), from the chain rule and evaluate it for quadratic cost.
demoIdeas: Perturb one output neuron's z by a small Δz (a 'demon' in the network) and watch the cost change by about δ·Δz, comparing the measured slope to BP1.

lessons.title: Propagating the Error Backward (BP2)
objectives: Derive BP2, δ^l = ((W^{l+1})ᵀ δ^{l+1}) ⊙ σ'(z^l), by writing z^{l+1} as a function of z^l and summing over all paths with the multivariable chain rule.
Explain why the transpose of the forward weight matrix appears and interpret backprop as sending error signals through the network in reverse.
keyEquations: \frac{\partial C}{\partial z^l_k} = \sum_j \frac{\partial C}{\partial z^{l+1}_j}\frac{\partial z^{l+1}_j}{\partial z^l_k}
demoIdeas: Animate a 3-layer network: forward pass fills neurons with activations left to right, then δ values flow right to left along the same edges, with edge thickness proportional to |w·δ|.

lessons.title: Gradients for Weights and Biases (BP3, BP4)
objectives: Derive BP3 (∂C/∂b_j^l = δ_j^l) and BP4 (∂C/∂w_jk^l = a_k^{l-1} δ_j^l) and write BP4 as the outer product δ^l (a^{l-1})ᵀ.
Explain from BP4 why weights out of low-activation neurons and into saturated neurons learn slowly.
demoIdeas: Show the weight-gradient matrix of one layer as the outer product of a δ column and an activation row, highlighting rows and columns that go to zero when units saturate or are inactive.

lessons.title: The Backpropagation Algorithm and Its Cost
objectives: State the full algorithm (forward pass, output error, backward pass, gradient assembly, minibatch averaging, update) in order.
Show that one backward pass costs about the same as one forward pass, whereas finite differences need one extra forward pass per parameter, and quantify the gap for a network with a million weights.
demoIdeas: Race backprop against finite differences as the parameter count slider grows: two bars show the number of forward-pass equivalents each method needs.

lessons.title: A Full Backprop Calculation on Paper
objectives: Carry out the forward and backward pass of a 2-2-1 sigmoid network for one training example entirely by hand, producing every δ and every weight gradient.
Check one of the hand-computed gradients with a central finite difference and explain why the agreement should be to O(h²).
demoIdeas: A fill-in-the-blanks worksheet network: the learner types each z, a, δ and gradient; each cell turns green when it matches the computed value, and a finite-difference check runs at the end.

lessons.title: Cross-Entropy and the Learning Slowdown
objectives: Show that with quadratic cost a saturated sigmoid output neuron learns slowly because δ^L contains σ'(z^L).
Derive that with cross-entropy cost the σ' factor cancels, giving δ^L = a^L - y, and explain why this makes 'very wrong' neurons learn fastest.

readings.title: Improving the way neural networks learn

demoIdeas: Train a single sigmoid neuron from a badly wrong start with quadratic vs cross-entropy cost; two cost-vs-epoch curves show the quadratic one stalling on a plateau.

units.title: Computational Graphs and Reverse-Mode Automatic Differentiation
units.summary: Backprop generalized: any computation is a graph of primitive operations with local derivatives, and reverse-mode autodiff evaluates all gradients of one scalar output in one backward sweep. This is the math behind the micrograd project.

lessons.title: Computational Graphs
objectives: Draw the computational graph of an expression such as L = (a·b + c)² · tanh(d), labelling every intermediate node.
Compute the local derivative on each edge and obtain ∂L/∂(each input) by multiplying along paths and summing over paths.

lectures.source: Andrej Karpathy, Neural Networks: Zero to Hero
lectures.title: Course page: all lectures in order

demoIdeas: Type an expression and see its computational graph laid out as nodes; clicking 'forward' fills in values, 'backward' fills in gradients node by node in reverse topological order.

lessons.title: Forward Mode vs Reverse Mode
objectives: Compute a derivative with forward-mode differentiation (dual numbers, tangents pushed forward) and the same derivative with reverse mode (adjoints pulled backward).

Explain forward mode as Jacobian-vector products and reverse mode as vector-Jacobian products, and derive that reverse mode wins when there are many inputs and one scalar output (a loss), forward mode when the reverse is true.
keyEquations: \bar v_j = \sum_{i\in\text{ch}(j)} \bar v_i\,\frac{\partial v_i}{\partial v_j},\quad \bar v \equiv \frac{\partial L}{\partial v}
demoIdeas: Toggle between forward and reverse mode on the same graph: forward mode needs one sweep per input (inputs light up one at a time), reverse mode one sweep for all inputs.

lessons.title: Local Gradient Rules, Fan-Out and Topological Order
objectives: State the backward rule for add, multiply, power, exp and tanh nodes (add routes the gradient unchanged, multiply swaps the inputs).
Explain why gradients must be accumulated (+=) when a node feeds several children, and show the wrong answer you get for b = a + a if they are overwritten.
Explain why the backward pass must visit nodes in reverse topological order, and construct that order for a small graph.
keyEquations: z = x + y:\ \bar x \mathrel{+}= \bar z,\ \bar y \mathrel{+}= \bar z
z = xy:\ \bar x \mathrel{+}= y\,\bar z,\ \bar y \mathrel{+}= x\,\bar z

lectures.source: Andrej Karpathy, Neural Networks: Zero to Hero
lectures.title: The spelled-out intro to neural networks and backpropagation: building micrograd

demoIdeas: A gate playground: wire add, multiply and tanh gates into a small circuit, run backward, and watch gradients split and merge; a toggle that overwrites instead of accumulating shows the fan-out bug.

lessons.title: Backprop Through Matrix Operations
objectives: Derive the backward pass of a linear layer Y = XW + b: ∂L/∂W = Xᵀ ∂L/∂Y, ∂L/∂X = ∂L/∂Y Wᵀ, ∂L/∂b = column sums of ∂L/∂Y, by checking index by index and by matching shapes.
Explain why broadcasting a bias in the forward pass becomes a sum over the batch in the backward pass.
keyEquations: \frac{\partial L}{\partial W} = X^\top\frac{\partial L}{\partial Y},\quad \frac{\partial L}{\partial X} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial Y}W^\top,\quad \frac{\partial L}{\partial b} = \Bigl(\frac{\partial L}{\partial Y}\Bigr)^{\!\top}\mathbf 1

lectures.source: Andrej Karpathy, Neural Networks: Zero to Hero
lectures.title: Building makemore Part 4: Becoming a Backprop Ninja (manual backprop through matrix ops)

demoIdeas: Shape puzzle: given the shapes of X, W and dL/dY, drag matrices and transposes into a product until the shapes match dL/dW, with the index sum shown for checking.

lessons.title: Gradient Checking and Numerical Pitfalls
objectives: Compare analytic and numerical gradients with the relative error |g_a - g_n| / max(|g_a|, |g_n|) and interpret typical thresholds.
Explain the trade-off in choosing h: truncation error O(h²) for central differences versus floating-point round-off that grows like ε_machine/h, and estimate the optimal h.
keyEquations: g_n = \frac{L(\theta + h e_i) - L(\theta - h e_i)}{2h}
demoIdeas: Plot the finite-difference error against h on log-log axes for a smooth function in float32 and float64: the V-shaped curve shows truncation error on the right and round-off on the left.

units.title: Optimizers and Loss Landscapes
units.summary: Beyond plain gradient descent: momentum as a damped heavy ball (underdamped vs overdamped motion), adaptive per-parameter step sizes (RMSProp, Adam), learning-rate schedules as annealing, and the geometry of high-dimensional loss surfaces, where saddle points (the transition states of a potential energy surface) outnumber local minima.

lessons.title: Momentum: The Heavy Ball with Friction
objectives: Derive the momentum update as the discretization of m θ'' + γ θ' = -∇L and identify the momentum coefficient β with the fraction of velocity kept per step.
Explain why momentum speeds progress along shallow valleys and damps zigzag across steep ones, and when too large β causes overshoot (underdamped oscillation).
Describe Nesterov momentum as evaluating the gradient at the look-ahead point.
demoIdeas: Race plain GD, momentum and Nesterov down a narrow curved valley (Rosenbrock), with a β slider that moves the ball from overdamped crawling to underdamped oscillation.

lessons.title: Adaptive Step Sizes: AdaGrad, RMSProp and Adam
objectives: Write the AdaGrad, RMSProp and Adam updates and explain each as dividing the step by a running estimate of the gradient's scale, per parameter.
Derive Adam's bias correction by computing E[m_t] for a constant gradient starting from m_0 = 0.
Explain adaptive methods as a diagonal preconditioner that partly undoes ill-conditioning, analogous to using mass-weighted or scaled coordinates.
demoIdeas: On a badly scaled bowl (one axis 100x steeper), compare SGD, RMSProp and Adam trajectories, with a readout of each method's effective per-axis step size.

lessons.title: Learning-Rate Schedules, Warmup and Annealing
objectives: Write step decay, exponential decay, cosine annealing and linear warmup as functions of the step t.
Explain why decaying the learning rate (lowering the SGD 'temperature') lets the iterate settle into a minimum, by analogy with simulated annealing and slow cooling in crystallization.

readings.title: Improving the way neural networks learn

demoIdeas: Pick a schedule (constant, step, cosine, warmup + cosine) and watch noisy SGD on a rugged landscape: the schedule plot and the loss trace update together, showing the final settling.

lessons.title: Loss Landscapes: Saddles, Plateaus and Flat Minima
objectives: Classify critical points by the signs of the Hessian eigenvalues and argue why, in high dimensions, saddle points vastly outnumber local minima.
Connect index-1 saddles to transition states on a potential energy surface, and explain why gradient noise helps escape them.
Explain the flat-versus-sharp minima picture of generalization and the caveat that sharpness depends on parametrization.

readings.title: Plateaus, Saddle Points and Other Flat Regions

demoIdeas: Explore a 2-D surface with a minimum, a saddle and a plateau: release balls with and without gradient noise and see where they stall; the Hessian eigenvalues at the cursor are shown live.

lessons.title: Diagnosing Training: Learning Curves and Hyperparameters
objectives: Read training and validation loss curves to diagnose underfitting, overfitting, a learning rate that is too high or too low, and a bug.
Explain why hyperparameters are chosen on a validation set and compare grid search with random search.

readings.title: Improving the way neural networks learn

demoIdeas: A gallery of learning-curve pairs (train/validation) to label as overfit, underfit, learning rate too high, or healthy, with instant feedback.

units.title: Training Deep Networks: Initialization, Gradients and Regularization
units.summary: Why deep networks are hard to train (products of Jacobians make gradients vanish or explode), how variance-preserving initialization and batch normalization fix it, and how weight decay (a harmonic restraint, or a Gaussian prior), dropout, early stopping and data augmentation keep a large network from memorizing its data.

lessons.title: Vanishing and Exploding Gradients
objectives: Show from BP2 that the gradient at layer l contains a product of (L - l) factors W^k σ'(z^k), and that with sigmoid (σ' ≤ 1/4) and small weights it shrinks geometrically.
Explain the exploding case (large weights) and why the two are 'unstable gradients' as a single phenomenon.

readings.title: Why are deep neural networks hard to train?

demoIdeas: A deep chain of layers drawn as a bar chart of gradient norm per layer; sliders for depth, weight scale and activation show the bars shrinking to nothing or blowing up.

lessons.title: Variance-Preserving Initialization (Xavier and He)
objectives: Derive that Var(z) = n_in Var(w) Var(x) for independent zero-mean weights and inputs, and choose Var(w) to keep activation variance constant from layer to layer.
Derive the He initialization Var(w) = 2/n_in for ReLU by accounting for half the units being zero, and state the Xavier/Glorot compromise between forward and backward passes.

readings.title: Improving the way neural networks learn

lectures.source: Andrej Karpathy, Neural Networks: Zero to Hero
lectures.title: Building makemore Part 3: Activations & Gradients, BatchNorm

demoIdeas: Push random data through a 20-layer network and show histograms of activations at each layer; switch between naive, Xavier and He initialization to watch them collapse, saturate or stay healthy.

lessons.title: Batch Normalization
objectives: Write the batch-norm transform (standardize over the batch, then scale by γ and shift by β) and explain why γ and β are learned.
Explain batch norm's effect on training stability and the difference between training-mode (batch statistics) and inference-mode (running averages) behavior.

lectures.source: Andrej Karpathy, Neural Networks: Zero to Hero
lectures.title: Building makemore Part 3: Activations & Gradients, BatchNorm

demoIdeas: Toggle batch norm on and off in a deep network and compare per-layer activation histograms and the training curve at a high learning rate.

lessons.title: Overfitting, Generalization and Double Descent
objectives: Diagnose overfitting from the gap between training and test error, and explain why a network with more parameters than examples can memorize random labels.
Describe the double-descent curve (test error vs model size peaks near the interpolation threshold, then falls) and how it complicates the classical bias-variance picture.

readings.title: Improving the way neural networks learn

demoIdeas: Fit noisy data with networks of growing width: a slider for width shows the fitted curve and a test-error-vs-width plot tracing the double-descent shape.

lessons.title: Weight Decay: L2 and L1 Regularization
objectives: Show that adding (λ/2)‖w‖² to the loss turns the update into w <- (1 - ηλ)w - η∇L, and interpret it as a harmonic restraint pulling weights to zero.
Derive L2 regularization as MAP estimation with a Gaussian prior on the weights, and L1 as a Laplace prior that drives weights exactly to zero.

readings.title: Improving the way neural networks learn

demoIdeas: Contour plot of a loss plus an L2 (circle) or L1 (diamond) constraint region: drag the penalty strength and see where the constrained optimum lands, often on an axis for L1.

lessons.title: Dropout and Ensembles
objectives: Describe dropout (randomly zeroing units with probability p during training, rescaling by 1/(1-p)) and why no units are dropped at test time.
Explain dropout as training an exponentially large ensemble of weight-sharing subnetworks, and why it discourages co-adapted features.

readings.title: Improving the way neural networks learn

demoIdeas: Watch a small network with dropout: each training step blacks out a random subset of units, while a side plot compares train/test error with and without dropout.

lessons.title: Early Stopping, Noise and Data Augmentation
objectives: Explain early stopping as choosing the number of steps on validation data, and show that for a quadratic loss it acts like L2 regularization with λ roughly 1/(η t).
Explain data augmentation and input noise as encoding known invariances (e.g. small rotations, shifts) and relate noise injection to an implicit penalty on the network's slope.

readings.title: Improving the way neural networks learn

demoIdeas: Train on a small data set while plotting train and validation loss; a marker shows the early-stopping point, and an 'augment' toggle adds jittered copies and moves the validation minimum.

units.title: Energy-Based Models: Hopfield Networks and Boltzmann Machines
units.summary: Networks defined by an energy function rather than a feedforward map. A Hopfield network is a zero-temperature Ising model whose couplings store memories; a Boltzmann machine is the same model at finite temperature, sampled by Gibbs (heat-bath Monte Carlo), whose learning rule needs averages over the Boltzmann distribution, which is why the partition function of P7 is the central obstacle.

lessons.title: Hopfield Networks as Zero-Temperature Ising Models
objectives: Write the Hopfield energy E = -½ Σ w_ij s_i s_j - Σ b_i s_i and map it term by term onto the Ising Hamiltonian (w_ij to J_ij, b_i to h_i, s_i = ±1 to spins).
Prove that an asynchronous update s_i <- sign(Σ_j w_ij s_j + b_i) never increases E when w is symmetric with zero diagonal, so the dynamics descend to a local minimum.
keyEquations: E(s) = -\tfrac12\sum_{i\ne j} w_{ij}s_is_j - \sum_i b_is_i \;\leftrightarrow\; H = -\sum_{\langle ij\rangle} J_{ij}\sigma_i\sigma_j - \sum_i h_i\sigma_i
demoIdeas: A grid of ±1 spins shown as black/white pixels with an energy readout: click 'update' and watch single spins flip one at a time while the energy trace only goes down.

lessons.title: Associative Memory: Hebbian Storage and Capacity
objectives: Store patterns with the Hebbian rule w_ij = (1/N) Σ_μ ξ_i^μ ξ_j^μ and show that each stored pattern is a fixed point when patterns are few and nearly orthogonal (signal plus crosstalk argument).
Explain recall from a corrupted cue, spurious states (mixtures and reversed patterns), and the capacity limit of about 0.14 N random patterns.
demoIdeas: Draw letters on a 10x10 grid to store them, then corrupt one with a noise slider and run the network: it snaps back to the stored letter, or into a spurious mixture when too many letters are stored.

lessons.title: Stochastic Units and the Boltzmann Distribution
objectives: Replace the deterministic Hopfield update with the stochastic rule p(s_i = 1) = σ(2h_i/T) for ±1 units and show that it samples the Boltzmann distribution p(s) = e^{-E(s)/T}/Z (Gibbs sampling, the heat-bath algorithm for the Ising model).
Explain the role of temperature: T to 0 recovers the Hopfield network, large T randomizes; compare to Metropolis Monte Carlo the chemist may have used.
Explain why Z = Σ_s e^{-E(s)/T} is a sum over 2^N states and therefore intractable, just as for the Ising model.
keyEquations: p(s_i = +1 \mid s_{\setminus i}) = \sigma\!\bigl(2h_i/T\bigr),\quad h_i = \sum_j w_{ij}s_j + b_i
demoIdeas: A 2-D Ising-like Boltzmann machine with a temperature slider: Gibbs sweeps run live, showing ordered domains at low T and noise at high T, with a histogram of visited energies.

lessons.title: Learning in Boltzmann Machines: Clamped vs Free Correlations
objectives: Derive the log-likelihood gradient ∂ ln p(v)/∂w_ij = ⟨s_i s_j⟩_data - ⟨s_i s_j⟩_model from p = e^{-E}/Z, identifying the second term as coming from ∂ ln Z/∂w_ij.
Interpret the two phases (clamped 'positive' and free-running 'negative') and explain why estimating the model term needs equilibrium sampling, the costly step.
Relate ∂ ln Z/∂w_ij = ⟨s_i s_j⟩ to the stat-mech identity that derivatives of ln Z with respect to a coupling give thermal averages.
demoIdeas: Train a tiny fully visible Boltzmann machine on a few binary patterns; bars compare the data correlations with the model's sampled correlations, converging as learning proceeds.

lessons.title: Restricted Boltzmann Machines and Contrastive Divergence
objectives: Write the RBM energy with a bipartite visible-hidden structure and show that the hidden units are conditionally independent given the visibles (and vice versa), so block Gibbs sampling is exact per layer.
Derive the free energy F(v) obtained by summing out the hidden units, and explain CD-k as approximating the model term with k Gibbs steps started at the data.
keyEquations: E(v,h) = -a^\top v - b^\top h - v^\top W h

project.title: micrograd from Scratch: A Tiny Autograd Engine and an MLP Trained with It
project.summary: Build a scalar reverse-mode automatic differentiation engine in plain Python (a Value class that records the computational graph and backpropagates through it), then build a neuron, layer and multilayer perceptron on top of it and train the MLP with your own SGD loop on a small 2-D classification problem, checking every gradient against finite differences.
goals: Turn the hand-derived backpropagation of Units 4–5 into working code whose gradients match finite differences.
Implement reverse-mode autodiff with correct fan-out accumulation and reverse topological ordering.
Train an MLP end to end with your own engine and see the decision boundary form.
Compare plain SGD with momentum, and observe the effect of learning rate and initialization on training.
steps: Write a Value class holding data, grad, its parent nodes and the operation that made it; support +, -, *, /, ** and exp, with operator overloading.
Give each operation a local _backward closure that accumulates (+=) gradients into its parents; add tanh and ReLU.
Implement backward(): build a topological order of the graph with a depth-first search, set the output grad to 1 and call _backward in reverse order.
Verify gradients on random expressions against central finite differences (relative error below 1e-6), including a node used twice.
Build Neuron, Layer and MLP classes on top of Value, with a parameters() method; use a sensible initialization scale.
Generate a 2-D data set (two moons or concentric circles), write a hinge or cross-entropy loss with L2 weight decay, and train with a minibatch SGD loop that zeroes gradients each step.
Plot the loss curve and the decision boundary at several epochs; add momentum and a learning-rate decay and compare.
Optional: cross-check one training step's gradients against PyTorch autograd on the same network and data.
project.stack: Python (standard library for the engine), NumPy and Matplotlib for data and plots; PyTorch optional, only to cross-check gradients
